name: Linoleic acid (omega-6)
short: Evidence is dietary, not from supplements, and mixed: one trial replacing saturated fat with linoleic acid after a coronary event found more deaths; cohort studies link higher intake to fewer deaths.
text: The cited evidence concerns linoleic acid in the diet rather than supplement capsules, and it points in both directions. In a randomised trial from 1966-73 in 458 men with a recent coronary event, replacing saturated fat with linoleic acid from safflower oil and margarine was followed by higher rates of death from all causes (17.6% versus 11.8%), cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease than in controls, who received no specific dietary instruction or study foods; when the same paper pooled this trial with other linoleic acid intervention trials, the trends toward more deaths from coronary heart disease and cardiovascular disease were not statistically significant, and the authors found no evidence of cardiovascular benefit. In contrast, a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies, which are observational and cannot show cause and effect, found that higher linoleic acid intake was associated with a modestly lower risk of death from all causes, cardiovascular disease and cancer. A meta-analysis of 30 randomised studies (1377 people) found that increasing dietary linoleic acid had no significant effect on blood inflammatory markers overall, although C-reactive protein might rise with larger increases in intake. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
